stem: What does the text mainly do with the belief stated in its first sentence?
stimulus: Engineers long assumed that glass is simply too brittle to bend. However, researchers have recently produced glass fibers thinner than a human hair that can be looped into a tight knot without snapping. Because the fibers are so thin, any flaws on their surfaces stay tiny, leaving cracks almost no room to start.
choices: It describes how researchers made very thin glass fibers.
It questions the belief that glass cannot bend.
It argues that glass is no longer brittle in any form.
It confirms the belief that glass breaks easily.
explanation: The first sentence gives a belief ('Engineers long assumed'), and 'However' signals that the author doubts it. The knotted fibers are evidence against that belief, so the text questions it. This one step, deciding whether the author agrees or disagrees with the opening view, is where every 'main purpose' question about a view-then-challenge text starts.

A.why: Most of the text is about the fibers, so this sounds right. But the fibers are only the evidence. You described what the text contains, not what it does to the opening belief.

C.why: The text shows that very thin fibers can bend. It never says glass has stopped being brittle in every form. You went past the evidence to a total rejection.

D.why: You missed the signal word 'However.' The text pushes back against the belief that glass can't bend. It does not support it.

stem: What does the text mainly do with the belief stated in its first sentence?
stimulus: Astronomers once thought that planets could form only around single stars like the Sun, reasoning that a second star's gravity would scatter the dust and gas from which planets are built. Yet telescopes have now detected dozens of planets orbiting pairs of stars. Some of these planets circle both stars at once, tracing wide and stable paths.
choices: It lists planets that telescopes have found orbiting star pairs.
It supports the idea that a second star scatters planet material.
It shows that most planets in the galaxy orbit two stars.
It challenges the view that only single stars can have planets.
explanation: 'Astronomers once thought' sets up a belief, and 'Yet' turns against it. The planets found around star pairs count as evidence that the old view was wrong, so the text challenges it. Spotting this belief-then-pivot pattern is the first move on real questions that ask for a text's main purpose.

A.why: The planets take up most of the text, but they are there to make a point about the old belief. You picked what the text talks about instead of what it is for.

B.why: That reasoning belongs to the old view the author is doubting. After 'Yet,' the text gives evidence against it, so the text does not back it up.

C.why: The text says 'dozens' of planets orbit star pairs. It says nothing about most planets in the galaxy. You stretched a small count into a claim about the whole galaxy.

stem: What does the text mainly do with the belief stated in its first sentence?
stimulus: Many people assume that washing with hot water removes more germs from the hands than washing with cool water does. In one test, however, volunteers washed their hands at several different water temperatures, and the amount of bacteria removed was about the same each time. What made the difference was scrubbing with soap for at least twenty seconds.
choices: It describes a test in which volunteers washed their hands.
It agrees that hot water removes more bacteria than cool water.
It casts doubt on the idea that hot water cleans hands better.
It claims that water temperature has no effect on health at all.
explanation: 'Many people assume' introduces a belief, and 'however' tells you the author doesn't accept it. The test results (the same amount of bacteria removed at every temperature) are evidence against it. So the text casts doubt on the belief. Finding the belief and the author's attitude toward it is what lets you answer 'main purpose' questions on texts like this.

A.why: This is true, and that's why it's tempting. But the test is the evidence, not the point. You described the content instead of the job it does.

B.why: The results showed about the same amount of bacteria removed at every temperature. You flipped the finding the author uses against the belief.

D.why: The text is only about how well handwashing removes bacteria. It makes no claim about water temperature and health in general. You turned a narrow finding into a sweeping one.

stem: What does the text mainly do with the belief stated in its first sentence?
stimulus: Coaches have long believed that stretching before a run protects athletes from injury. But when researchers split runners into a group that stretched before training and a group that did not, injury rates in the two groups were nearly identical. Stretching may still improve flexibility, the researchers note, but it does not appear to prevent injuries.
choices: It questions the belief that stretching prevents injury.
It describes a study that compared two groups of runners.
It argues that runners should never stretch for any reason.
It confirms the belief that stretching keeps runners safe.
explanation: 'Coaches have long believed' states the belief, and 'But' turns against it. The nearly identical injury rates are evidence that stretching doesn't prevent injury, so the text questions the belief. The real exam version of this pattern asks for the text's main purpose, and you can't answer it until you've made this one call.

B.why: The study fills most of the text, so it feels like the main point. But it is there to test the coaches' belief. You named what the text contains, not what it is for.

C.why: The researchers say stretching may still help flexibility. The text doubts one specific benefit and doesn't reject stretching altogether. You read a narrow doubt as a total rejection.

D.why: You missed 'But.' The two groups had nearly the same injury rates, which is evidence against the belief, not for it.
